title: Sultanate of Selangor
capsule: The Sultanate of Selangor was founded on the western coast of the Malay Peninsula when Raja Lumu, a Bugis prince from South Sulawesi, was installed as Sultan Salehuddin around 1766 after Bugis warriors had dominated the region since the 1740s. The sultanate's wealth rested on control of tin-bearing river valleys, particularly the Klang and Selangor rivers, which attracted Chinese mining labor and generated revenues from trade with regional and European merchants. Internecine succession conflicts in the 1860s–1870s, combined with Chinese mining faction wars, drew British intervention; the 1874 Treaty of Pangkor established British oversight in the neighboring Perak, and Selangor accepted a British Resident in 1874, surrendering effective sovereignty. The attested window (1744–1877) covers the sultanate from its Bugis foundations through the onset of British indirect rule.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The core territories around the Klang and Selangor river valleys are well attested, but outer boundaries of the sultanate's shifting control over interior tin-mining areas are only approximately documented in this pre-colonial period.
